strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: fine-tuning diffusion models for non-differentiable rewards common in biomolecular design (DSSP-based structure matching, AlphaFold-based ipTM, QuickVina docking), where reward backpropagation is inapplicable.

The algorithmic framing — iterative distillation of soft-optimal policies via value-weighted MLE with off-policy roll-ins and lazy target updates — is coherent, clearly motivated, and grounded in established RL theory (relative entropy policy search, advantage-weighted regression), with the PPO-as-reverse-KL connection stated as a theorem and proved in the appendix.

Empirically broad evaluation across three distinct domains (protein sequence design, regulatory DNA design, small molecule design) with appropriate baselines (DDPO, DDPP, DRAKES, SFT, Best-of-N) and orthogonal naturalness metrics (pLDDT, 3-mer correlation, ATAC-Acc, NLL, FCD/SNN/NSPDK).

Includes useful ablations: lazy update interval K (Table 8), roll-in mixture βs (Figure 4), reward-diversity trade-off analysis (Figures 5-6), and combination with Best-of-N inference-time sampling (Tables 6-7), showing orthogonality of the method.
ATAC-Acc evaluation addresses reward over-optimization concerns, and the paper reports diversity alongside reward, which is often missing in reward-fine-tuning papers. Code is released.

Results show substantial gains: e.g., β-sheet% 0.83 vs 0.81 (DDPO), Pred-Activity 8.28 vs 7.38 (DDPO) and 6.44 (DRAKES), and notably larger margins on binder design (ipTM 0.82 vs 0.79 on PD-L1, with better diversity than DDPO in some settings).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core objective is essentially value-weighted MLE (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019) combined with the soft-optimal policy framing of Uehara et al. (2025a) and the r(x̂0) soft-value approximation already implicitly used in test-time guidance methods (Chung et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). The main contribution is adaptation of these known components to the fine-tuning setting; the paper is transparent about this but the delta is incremental.

The forward-KL vs reverse-KL argument for stability is asserted more than demonstrated: Theorem 1 is straightforward algebra, and no theoretical or empirical analysis directly isolates the contribution of the KL direction versus the off-policy roll-in versus the lazy target update. An ablation swapping forward/reverse KL in the VIDD framework would substantially strengthen the central claim.

The soft value approximation r(x̂0(xt)) replaces a conditional expectation with a single-sample posterior mean substitute; its quality and the resulting bias in the value-weighted objective are not analyzed, and no comparison against a learned value function or Monte Carlo estimator is provided.

Some experimental results raise concerns about robustness and reproducibility: ATAC-Acc for VIDD (0.820 ± 0.384) is wildly variable and dramatically better than all baselines (~0.0-0.3), while Table 8 shows this metric collapses to ~0.0-0.08 for K ∈ {1, 10, 20}; such extreme sensitivity to a single hyperparameter undermines claims of stability. Number of seeds and statistical protocol are under-specified.

No wet-lab or downstream experimental validation; all rewards are computational oracles (Enformer predictor, AlphaFold2-Multimer, QuickVina), so true biological/functional validity of the designs remains unverified — a common but significant limitation for the biomolecular design claims.

Diversity drops substantially for VIDD on binder tasks (0.52-0.55 vs ~0.90 pre-trained), and the paper does not quantify or bound this mode-concentration; the forward-KL mode-covering argument would predict better behavior than observed.

Hyperparameters (α, βs, K, learning rate) appear task-specific and validation-selected, which complicates fair comparison with baselines whose hyperparameters may be less tuned; compute-matched comparison details (e.g., reward queries per method) are not provided despite reward evaluation cost being flagged as a key concern in the limitations.

strengths: The problem setting is well-motivated: fine-tuning diffusion models with non-differentiable rewards (docking scores, DSSP, AlphaFold-based metrics) is genuinely important for scientific design applications, and the paper clearly positions itself against both differentiable-reward backpropagation and on-policy RL methods.

The algorithmic framing is coherent: collecting off-policy roll-ins, simulating reward-weighted soft-optimal policies during roll-out, and performing KL-based distillation with lazy target updates is a sensible design that connects to established ideas (value-weighted MLE / advantage-weighted regression, entropy-regularized MDPs).

Theorem 1 provides a clean connection between the PPO-style objective used by DDPO/DPOK and reverse KL divergence to the soft-optimal policy, which usefully explains the mode-seeking behavior of prior methods.

Empirical coverage is broad: three distinct biomolecular domains (protein sequence, regulatory DNA, small molecule) with multiple reward functions, several baselines, ablations on the lazy update interval K and roll-in mixture β, plus combination with Best-of-N inference-time techniques.
Reproducibility appears reasonably addressed: hyperparameters are tabulated, hardware/software described, licenses listed, and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core algorithm is essentially reward-weighted maximum likelihood / advantage-weighted regression (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019) applied iteratively to diffusion denoising policies, with a lazy target update borrowed from standard RL practice (target networks, policy iteration). The soft-optimal policy construction is well known from the guidance/alignment literature the authors themselves cite (Uehara et al., 2025a). The contribution feels like a combination of known components rather than a fundamentally new idea.

A significant theory-practice mismatch is not adequately addressed. The soft value function in Eq. (3) is defined as an expectation under the pre-trained trajectory distribution, but in Algorithm 1 the roll-out policy p_out (a periodically updated student model) is used instead, and the value is approximated by the crude point estimate v̂ = r(x̂0(xt)) (posterior-mean substitution). The bias introduced by this approximation is never quantified or theoretically justified, even though it is central to the method.

The 'forward KL vs. reverse KL' story is overstated. Theorem 1 is a straightforward algebraic identity, and the actual optimized objective (Eq. 7) is a value-weighted MLE whose weights depend on the current model — it is only loosely a forward-KL objective ('more closely resembles'). The empirical claim that this divergence choice is the source of stability is asserted rather than isolated; there is no ablation swapping the divergence to verify the causal claim.

Evidence for the headline stability/sample-efficiency claims is weak. No wall-clock or reward-query budget comparisons are reported despite claims of sample efficiency; baseline hyperparameters (DDPO, DDPP) tuning effort is not described, raising fairness concerns given that PPO-style methods are notoriously hyperparameter-sensitive.

Several results show concerning variance and possible over-optimization artifacts: the ATAC-Acc value for VIDD (0.820 ± 0.384) has an extremely wide confidence interval, and the K ablation (Table 8) shows ATAC-Acc collapsing to 0.000 for K=1, suggesting fragile behavior that is not discussed seriously. Diversity consistently drops for VIDD relative to pre-trained models on protein tasks, and the naturalness argument relies partly on secondary metrics computed by the same oracles used for reward.

Missing baselines: comparisons are confined to DDPO, DDPP, SFT, and Best-of-N. Other relevant fine-tuning approaches for discrete/scientific diffusion (e.g., methods cited in Section 1.1 such as Rector-Brooks variants, policy-gradient methods for discrete diffusion by Zekri and Boullé, or inference-time steering baselines like SMC/DPS beyond the molecule task) are absent or inconsistently included across tasks.

Presentation issues undermine polish: Algorithm 1 line 9 appears to contain a typo ('If S%K = 0' should presumably be s%K), notation is inconsistently defined (pT (·|·), the double citation of Uehara et al. 2025a/2025b with identical arXiv IDs), and Figure 1's caption contains a garbled sentence. The roll-in/roll-out/distillation decomposition, while clearly intended, adds notational overhead that obscures that the final update is a simple weighted log-likelihood ascent.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: fine-tuning diffusion models with non-differentiable reward functions (e.g., DSSP, AlphaFold-derived, AutoDock Vina), where direct reward backpropagation is inapplicable.

The framework is clearly grounded in the entropy-regularized MDP view of diffusion models, with a coherent derivation of the value-weighted MLE / forward-KL distillation objective (Eqs. 4-7) and a clean theoretical result (Theorem 1) connecting the PPO objective to reverse-KL minimization.

The off-policy roll-in with a mixture of pre-trained and lazy-updated roll-out policies is a sensible and well-argued design choice for stability, supported by ablations on the lazy update interval K (Table 8) and the roll-in mixture beta_s (Figure 4).

Empirically broad evaluation across three distinct biomolecular domains (protein sequences, regulatory DNA, small molecules) with appropriate baselines (DRAKES, DDPO, DDPP, SFT, Best-of-N), plus naturalness/robustness checks such as the orthogonal ATAC-Acc reward, which strengthens the over-optimization argument.

Good supplementary material: hyperparameter tables, license information, diversity/novelty/validity metrics for molecules, reward-diversity trade-off analysis, training curves, and released source code supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is incremental. The core components (soft-optimal policies, value-weighted MLE, off-policy roll-ins) are largely borrowed from the RL literature (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019) and from inference-time guidance methods (Chung et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024); the contribution is primarily adapting these to the fine-tuning setting rather than a fundamentally new technique.

There is a theoretical gap between the defined soft value function (Eq. 3, a conditional expectation over continuations) and the practical approximation v(x) = r(x0_hat(x)) (posterior mean of the one-step denoised output). The bias of this approximation is not analyzed, and no empirical comparison against Monte Carlo or learned value functions is provided.

Several results are mixed or noisy: VIDD's 3-mer Corr on DNA (0.162) is substantially worse than DDPO (0.879), ATAC-Acc has very large variance (0.820 ± 0.384), and the molecule docking gain over DDPO is modest (9.4 vs 8.5). Diversity drops notably relative to the pre-trained model (e.g., 0.52 vs 0.91 on binder tasks), and the reward-diversity trade-off, while acknowledged, is not fully resolved.

The claimed benefits in stability and sample efficiency compared to PPO-based methods are argued qualitatively but not rigorously quantified (e.g., wall-clock time, number of reward evaluations, hyperparameter sensitivity curves across methods).
Theorem 1 follows from straightforward algebra and mainly re-frames the known connection between entropy-regularized objectives and reverse KL; its technical depth is limited.

Evaluation relies on proxy/simulation oracles (ESMFold, AlphaFold2, Enformer, docking scores); no wet-lab or downstream functional validation is presented, which is a standard caveat for this line of work.
Writing quality is uneven, with grammatical errors (e.g., 'slight abust of notation', 'rather, which contribute', 'We learn two These datasets') that should be corrected before camera-ready.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: fine-tuning diffusion models with non-differentiable, scientific reward functions where direct backpropagation (DRAKES-style) is impossible.

The proposed VIDD framework is well-motivated: framing fine-tuning as iterative distillation of soft-optimal policies, using off-policy roll-ins, value-weighted MLE distillation, and lazy target updates to improve stability and sample efficiency compared to on-policy PPO-style methods (DDPO/DDPP).

Theoretical analysis is reasonable: Theorem 1 connects the PPO-style objective to reverse KL minimization, providing a clean justification for the forward-KL/distillation perspective, and Appendix B derives the value-weighted MLE objective from the KL distillation loss.

Empirical evaluation is broad and mostly convincing, spanning protein sequence design (SS-match, binder design with AlphaFold2-Multimer), regulatory DNA design (including the DRAKES baseline with a differentiable reward), and small molecule design (QuickVina2 docking). VIDD consistently outperforms fine-tuning baselines.

The appendix contains substantial supporting material: ablations on lazy update interval K, regularization coefficient alpha, roll-in mixture beta, soft value estimation variants (posterior mean vs Monte Carlo vs learned critic), robustness to noisy rewards, and qualitative visualizations of generated structures.

A useful distinction is drawn and empirically examined between the optimized reward and independent naturalness metrics (ATAC-Acc, 3-mer correlation, pLDDT, NLL, diversity), partially addressing reward over-optimization concerns.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest: the core algorithm is essentially value-weighted maximum likelihood (AWR, Peters et al. 2019; Peng et al. 2019) instantiated for diffusion models, with the posterior-mean soft value approximation borrowed from test-time methods (SVDD, Li et al. 2024) and lazy target updates being standard RL practice. The contribution is more a careful combination of existing ideas than a fundamentally new technique.

Evidence of possible reward over-optimization is not fully resolved. The jump in ipTM from 0.148 (pre-trained) to 0.82 (VIDD) is dramatic and the optimized reward is itself an AlphaFold2-Multimer output, raising the possibility that the model exploits the structure-prediction oracle. No wet-lab or independent experimental validation is provided for any designed binder.

Some naturalness metrics degrade substantially under VIDD (e.g., 3-mer correlation of 0.162 vs ~0.89-0.95 for baselines on DNA; diversity drops on binder tasks), suggesting distribution shift that is downplayed. The paper argues this reflects exploration, but a stricter analysis of sample quality would strengthen the claims.

The comparison with DRAKES on DNA is inherently asymmetric since DRAKES backpropagates through a differentiable reward; including it is informative but the paper's headline claims of 'superior reward optimization' should be more carefully scoped to the non-differentiable setting.

The theoretical contribution is light: Theorem 1 is a straightforward algebraic derivation, and there is no formal analysis of convergence, stability, or approximation error of the posterior-mean value substitution (the bias of v_t ≈ r(x̂_0) is not bounded or quantified).

Hyperparameter sensitivity remains a practical concern: results depend non-monotonically on K and task-dependently on beta_s and alpha (per Tables 9, 16-20), which somewhat undercuts the claimed robustness advantage over PPO-style baselines; the authors acknowledge this only in limitations.

Missing ablations/comparisons would be useful: e.g., direct comparison against the value-weighted fine-tuning baseline with on-policy roll-ins only (to isolate the benefit of off-policy roll-ins), and combinations with other fine-tuning families (e.g., DDPO with large KL penalties).

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: the method is evaluated across three distinct biomolecular domains (protein sequence, regulatory DNA, small molecule), with multiple reward types including genuinely non-differentiable ones (DSSP, AlphaFold2 ipTM, QuickVina docking), which is a reasonable testbed for the stated problem.

VIDD achieves higher rewards than DDPO/DDPP/SFT baselines on most tasks, and ablations over lazy-update interval K, regularization coefficient α, roll-in mixture βs, and value estimator choice (posterior mean vs. Monte Carlo) are provided.

The connection between the PPO objective and reverse KL to the soft-optimal policy (Theorem 1) is correct and cleanly stated, and the writing situates the method within the value-weighted MLE / soft-Optimal policy literature reasonably well.

The paper is transparent about limitations (reward noise sensitivity, hyperparameter sensitivity), and reports orthogonal metrics (ATAC-Acc, 3-mer correlation, NLL, pDockQ) to probe reward over-optimization.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The algorithm is essentially value-weighted MLE (Peters et al. 2010; Peng et al. 2019, AWR) applied to diffusion fine-tuning, using the posterior-mean value approximation v(xt) ≈ r(x̂0(xt)) already established in test-time guidance methods (Chung et al. 2022; Li et al. 2024 SVDD). The main contribution—amortizing SVDD-style guidance into a fine-tuning procedure via iterative distillation—is an incremental combination of known components. Theorem 1 is a straightforward derivation, not a substantive theoretical contribution.

The central stability claims are undermined by the paper's own ablations. Reported results swing wildly with hyperparameters: on PD-L1, reward ranges from 0.19 to 0.91 depending on the lazy update interval K, and from 0.44 to 0.91 with α; on IFNAR2 from 0.12 to 0.51 with K. This level of sensitivity contradicts the headline claim that the off-policy, forward-KL formulation 'enhances training stability', and suggests the method is highly tuned per task.

Mode collapse concerns are not resolved. Diversity drops substantially for VIDD (e.g., 0.52 vs. 0.90 for the pretrained model on binding tasks; 0.162 3-mer correlation vs. 0.887 for DRAKES on DNA). The forward-KL argument against mode collapse is asserted but not substantiated by analysis, and the paper effectively concedes a reward–diversity trade-off rather than demonstrating mode-coverage.

Statistical soundness is questionable in places: ATAC-Acc for VIDD is reported as 0.820 ± 0.384 (enormous variance, effectively uninformative), and it is unclear how many independent seeds underlie the confidence intervals; some diversity and correlation columns report no uncertainty at all. Compute-matched comparisons with DDPO/DDPP (which the paper criticizes for sample inefficiency) are not shown.

The forward-KL framing is somewhat overstated. Because the teacher is lazily updated from the student, the actual iterated procedure's divergence properties relative to the target distribution exp(r/α)p_pre are not analyzed; the stated equivalence is between the fixed-teacher distillation objective and the KL objective, not the full algorithm.

The greedy argmax-decoding value approximation r(x̂0(xt)) is a crude, biased estimate of the soft value; while the paper shows it outperforms small-M Monte Carlo empirically, no analysis is given of the bias introduced, and the results in Table 9/17/18 suggest the whole scheme is fragile to this choice.

Baselines are uneven: DRAKES is included only for the differentiable DNA task, no fine-tuning baselines are run on the protein β-sheet/molecule tasks beyond DDPO/DDPP/SFT, and Best-of-N is dismissed as impractical yet performs surprisingly well relative to baselines. Reproducibility details (code release, seeds) are not stated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: fine-tuning diffusion models under non-differentiable reward functions is a genuinely important and practical problem in biomolecular design, and the paper positions itself well against both gradient-based (DRAKES, reward backprop) and RL-based (DDPO, DDPP) alternatives.

The off-policy, forward-KL (value-weighted MLE) formulation is a sensible and well-argued alternative to on-policy reverse-KL policy gradient methods, with a clean derivation connecting the distillation objective (4) to the practical loss (5), and a simple but useful Theorem 1 connecting the PPO-style objective to reverse KL.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three distinct domains (protein sequence, regulatory DNA, small molecule), with multiple relevant baselines (SFT, DDPO, DDPP, DRAKES, Best-of-N) and additional independent evaluation metrics (ATAC-Acc, 3-mer correlation, NLL, pTM/pDockQ, molecular diversity/validity metrics) that probe beyond the optimized reward.

Extensive ablations and robustness analyses: lazy update interval K, regularization coefficient α, roll-in mixture β_s, posterior-mean vs. Monte Carlo vs. learned value functions, and a synthetic noise-reward study — these go beyond what most similar papers provide and support reproducibility.

Honest discussion of trade-offs: the paper openly reports where VIDD sacrifices diversity, naturalness (3-mer Corr), and NLL, and discusses reward-model over-optimization and noise sensitivity in the limitations section.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core algorithm is essentially advantage/value-weighted maximum likelihood (AWR, Peters et al. 2010; Peng et al. 2019) applied iteratively to diffusion denoising, with a lazy target update (a standard RL trick) and a posterior-mean soft-value approximation already adopted in test-time methods (SVDD, Li et al. 2024) — the paper itself acknowledges this. The contribution is a careful combination rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Theorem 1 is straightforward algebra (a few lines of KL expansion in Appendix A) and does not constitute a substantial theoretical contribution; no convergence, stability, or sample-complexity analysis is provided to support the claimed stability advantages of forward KL.

Surprisingly large gaps over baselines (e.g., ipTM of 0.82 vs. ~0.19–0.38 for DDPO/DDPP on PD-L1) invite scrutiny: it is unclear whether baseline hyperparameters were tuned comparably, and results appear to be from single runs (95% CI is reported but the number of independent seeds is not stated). Performance curves in Fig. 5 also suggest high variance and non-monotone behavior.

Signs of possible distribution degradation/over-optimization: on DNA, 3-mer Corr drops from 0.887 (DRAKES) to 0.162 and NLL worsens relative to the pretrained model; ATAC-Acc (independent metric) drops sharply for some settings. The ipTM reward is itself a learned proxy oracle, so the huge ipTM gains may partly reflect exploitation of the surrogate rather than genuinely better binders; no wet-lab or orthogonal validation of binding is provided.

The off-policy claim is somewhat overstated: the roll-out policy is refreshed from the student every K steps, so the framework is closer to a slowly-updated on-policy scheme; the empirical benefit of the off-policy mechanism relative to simply lowering the update frequency of an on-policy method is not fully disentangled.

Experiments are limited to relatively small pretrained models (EvoDiff 38M, GDSS) and a single docking target (parp1) for molecules; scalability to larger or continuous diffusion models (e.g., structure-based design) remains untested, which narrows the claimed generality of the framework.
